title: High-NA vectorial hologram optimization
authors: Michael Wischert, Fiona Hellstern, Paul Uerlings, Tilman Pfau, Stephan Welte, Ralf Klemt
abstract: We present a vectorial phase-only framework for the gradient-based optimization of computer-generated holograms. Our approach addresses a critical limitation in high numerical aperture (NA) optical systems, where standard scalar approximations often experience significant fidelity degradation. We highlight the limitations of scalar diffraction models (Fraunhofer and Debye) at high NA for representative classes of target intensities, namely tweezer arrays and extended flat-top profiles. Using a differentiable Richards-Wolf forward model, we numerically demonstrate stable algorithmic convergence and the generation of highly uniform intensity profiles in the deep non-paraxial regime. At NA=0.9, Richards-Wolf (RW) optimization reaches flat-top and tweezer uniformities of 99.97 % and 99.98 %, respectively, with a mean tweezer ellipticity of $\varepsilon=$1.007, while scalar forward models show target-dependent degradation in plateau fidelity or focal geometry. Furthermore, because the RW model returns the full vectorial field, the same framework can optimize objectives that depend on local polarization. We demonstrate this for a polarization-sensitive optical-dipole-potential target, where direct RW-potential optimization reduces the mean normalized residual by more than an order of magnitude when including vector and tensor light-shift terms.
summary: This paper develops a full vectorial framework to optimize computer-generated holograms for high numerical aperture optics, overcoming fidelity losses associated with standard scalar approximations. By using the Richards-Wolf model in a gradient-based optimization loop, the authors demonstrate superior control over target intensity and polarization structure compared to simpler models. This has significant implications for advanced quantum trapping and light-matter interaction experiments.
main_problem: The study addresses the fidelity degradation when optimizing computer-generated holograms (CGHs) for high numerical aperture (NA) optical systems using standard scalar approximations instead of full vectorial models.
main_result: Using a differentiable Richards-Wolf model, the optimization successfully generates highly uniform intensity profiles and allows for the direct optimization of objectives dependent on local polarization state, significantly outperforming scalar methods at high NA.
method: The authors employ gradient-based nonlinear optimization techniques (e.g., L-BFGS) applied to a differentiable Richards-Wolf forward model to find the optimal phase modulation required to match a target intensity profile.
model_or_system: The system involves using Spatial Light Modulators (SLMs) as programmable pupil-plane phase elements in high-NA focusing geometries. The propagation is modeled by comparing the full vectorial Richards-Wolf (RW) formalism against scalar approximations like Debye and Fraunhofer models.
key_observables: Target uniformity, mean tweezer ellipticity ($\epsilon$), and reduction in normalized residual for polarization-sensitive potentials.
important_parameters: High Numerical Aperture (NA=0.9), target geometries (tweezer arrays, flat-top profiles), and the comparison between vectorial vs. scalar light propagation models.
main_assumptions: The surrounding medium is assumed to have a refractive index of n=1; scalar models are fundamentally limited as they ignore polarization mixing effects crucial at high NA.
figures_summary: Figures compare intensity profiles for tweezer and flat-top targets, contrasting the superior uniformity achieved via RW optimization against the fidelity loss observed using scalar approximations (Fraunhofer/Debye).
paper_structure: The paper establishes the limitations of scalar models at high NA, details the implementation of gradient-based optimization using the full vectorial Richards-Wolf model, demonstrates quantitative improvements in target shaping metrics (uniformity, ellipticity), and extends the framework to polarization-sensitive objectives.
why_interesting: This work directly tackles the computational optics challenges inherent in modern quantum trapping and manipulation techniques that rely on precise light field control at high NA. The rigorous comparison between scalar and vectorial models is crucial for designing next-generation optical elements for AMO experiments.
